content: Logical tests and automatically calculated fields, such as age derived from the date of birth, are essential tools for ensuring data accuracy. It is critical to identify errors in national datasets by running queries, even though many of these errors can be prevented during data entry. An implausible value refers to an unrealistic entry in a database, such as a patient in 2012 being recorded with a birth date of 01/01/1848. Systems should define acceptable ranges for numeric and date fields and enforce these during data entry. Outliers and values outside acceptable ranges should be identified through methods like frequency charts or distribution analysis. Duplicate records occur when more than one entry in the national database refers to the same tuberculosis (TB) case. Unique identifiers, such as identity card numbers or social security numbers, can help prevent duplicates. If unavailable, sub-national or local patient identifiers, like TB register numbers, can be used, provided there are standard procedures to ensure only one code is assigned per case and to manage patient movement between locations with different numbering systems. De-duplication algorithms often rely on probabilistic matching of variables like name, sex, address, date of birth, and diagnosis date. These algorithms account for variations in spelling and recording and require high completeness rates for these fields. Potential duplicates identified by the algorithm must be manually verified to confirm whether they represent the same TB case or separate cases. To assess benchmarks, data sources and collection methods should include records of notified TB cases in the national database for the assessment year, system documentation, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and automated checks performed during data entry. Analysis should determine whether standard procedures are in place to identify and correct records with misclassified, implausible, inconsistent, or missing data. If not, additional tests may be required during data quality checks. Running system data quality checks on the national dataset for the assessment year is essential. De-duplication procedures should be examined, and if feasible, the country’s duplicate detection algorithm should be applied to the national dataset. In cases of duplicate records, only one should be counted as the extra duplicate. However, de-duplication often involves a combination of automated and manual checks, which can be time-consuming. Alternatively, records of the de-duplication process can be reviewed to determine how many potential duplicates remain unresolved. If a flagging system is used, the percentage of flagged records should be calculated. Key limitations include variability in data structures and checks across countries, the inability to assess duplicate cases without sufficient patient-specific information, and the challenge of detecting certain data entry errors without source document verification. For example, a birth date of 01/01/1956 mistakenly recorded as 01/01/1965 may not be identifiable at the national level. A data audit may be conducted if deemed useful. Interpretation of results involves determining whether standard data checking and correction procedures are in place. If <1% of records are potential duplicate TB cases, the third benchmark is satisfied. Meeting all benchmarks indicates the standard is met. Partial satisfaction of benchmarks indicates the standard is only partially met. Failure to meet the first benchmark, regardless of the others, means the standard is not met. Recommended actions for unmet standards include implementing suggested data quality checks, providing feedback to sub-national users, highlighting data quality in regular meetings, developing SOPs and training materials, and securing senior management commitment to data quality. Additional options include cross-checking national and sub-national datasets, establishing a national data management unit, conducting operational research to improve data quality, and addressing benchmark gaps with an investment plan. Examples from the Netherlands and the United Kingdom illustrate effective data quality practices. The Netherlands uses a web-based TB notification system with data validation routines to prevent implausible entries. Data managers review new cases daily, and inconsistencies are sent back to local staff for clarification. The system satisfied all benchmarks in 2011. In the UK, Public Health England (PHE) manages a national web-based surveillance system. Mandatory fields like notification date and birth date must be 100% complete. Data validation checks prevent errors, and quarterly reports identify data problems. PHE investigates and addresses unmet targets, such as improving completeness of previous diagnosis and treatment fields. De-duplication is performed annually, and laboratory isolates are matched to notifications to ensure all detected cases are reported. Regular checks include follow-up of drug-resistant cases and de-notified cases with confirmed laboratory results.
